catalog_quote: [Verstraete 2021: 17] There are three indications that the original stress system in Umpithamu must have been one that was left-aligned, with a leftmost stress rule. The first indication is local, relating to Umpithamu’s closest relatives. Most other Middle Paman languages for which we have a reliable description of word stress have a system of this kind: this is the case, for instance, in Wik Mungkan (Kilham 1974), Kugu Nganhcara (Smith & Johnson 2000), Wik Ngathan (Sutton 1978) and possibly also Umpila (Thompson 1988).5 [fn.5] There are some complications in Umpila relating to syllable weight (due to the occurrence of vowel length beyond the first syllable). [Blevins 2025: 142] One of these is Kugu Nganhcara, a Pama-Nyungan language of Australia, as described by Smith & Johnson (2000). new_statements.rule_in_words: Second-hand: according to Verstraete's reading of Smith & Johnson (2000), Kugu Nganhcara has a left-aligned stress system with primary stress assigned by a leftmost rule, i.e. on the word-initial syllable, like its Wik/Middle Paman relatives.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing stated for Kugu Nganhcara (Verstraete only notes generically that some Pama-Nyungan descriptions report alternating secondary stress).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level primary stress ('description of word stress'); the statement is a one-line typological characterisation in a paper about Umpithamu, not a description of Kugu Nganhcara itself. The primary description (Smith & Johnson 2000, HAL 5) could not be opened.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog wikn1246 'Wikngenchera' [wua] is the exonym/ISO entry for Kugu Nganhcara (Wik-Ngenchera, Kugu-Nganycharra; AUSTLANG Y59), a cluster of six patrilects that Glottolog also lists separately: Kugu Uwanh (kuku1280), Kugu Muminh (kuku1283), Kugu Mu'inh (kuku1282), Kugu Ugbanh (kuku1281), Kugu Yi'anh/Mangk, Wik Iyanh (wiki1239). The primary grammar (Smith & Johnson 2000) is filed by Glottolog under kuku1280; Smith & Johnson's data come mainly from Kugu Uwanh (Smith) and Kugu Muminh (Johnson) informants (Smith & Johnson 1986: fieldwork note). Sutton 1978, the source named by the earlier scan, describes Wik-Ngathana (wikn1245) and does not state stress for Kugu Nganhcara. Any catalog entry should be shared with / cross-referenced to kuku1280-kuku1283.

sources.note: Appendix 1 (p.234ff) 'In general, primary stress falls on the first vowel of any word..' but the description is explicitly scoped to Wik-Ngathana (and 'would generally hold good, at the structural level, for Wik-Ngatharra'); ch. IV 'Linguistic relationships' mentions the Kugu dialects only for final-vowel retention, stop voicing and retroflexes, with no stress statement for Kugu-Nganycharra. Cites Johnson 1974 BA Hons thesis on Kugu Uwanh sound patterns. So the earlier scan's named source does not actually cover this language's stress.
